background.definition: Milia are 1 to 3 mm, white to yellow keratinous cysts that can arise spontaneously (primary) or in association with various diseases, medications, or trauma (secondary).

list.listitem: Up to 50% of neonates have milia, likely due to prominent sebaceous gland activity.

Group 1: Congenital milia occur in approximately 40% to 50% of newborns with no racial or sexual predilection. Lesions favor the face, upper trunk, and upper extremities and tend to spontaneously resolve within weeks to months. Common oral variants in neonates include Epstein's pearls on the gum margins (up to 85% of neonates) and Bohn's nodules on the hard palate.
Group 2: Benign primary milia, favoring the cheeks and eyelids, are extremely common in all ages. Acquired lesions tend to persist longer than congenital lesions.
Group 3: Milia occurring over reddish plaques on the head and neck (Milia en plaque), grouped nodular milia, and multiple eruptive milia are extremely rare.
Milia evaluation and treatment are very common primary or secondary complaints among visits to dermatologists.
Primary milia are thought to arise from sebaceous glands in the lower infundibular portion of the hair follicle, while secondary milia are thought to arise from disrupted sweat glands.

Secondary milia can be associated with blistering diseases such as porphyria cutanea tarda (OMIM 176100), Kindler syndrome (OMIM 173650), and various forms of epidermolysis bullosa. Genodermatoses associated with milia include Brooke-Spiegler syndrome (OMIM 605041), Rombo syndrome (OMIM 180730), Bazex-Dupre-Christol syndrome (OMIM 301845), Papillon-League-Psaume syndrome (OMIM 311200), Hereditary vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2A (OMIM 277440), Gorlin syndrome (OMIM 109400), Pachyonychia congenita type 2 (OMIM 167210), Atrichia with papular lesions (OMIM 209500), and Familial milia and absent dermatoglyphics (OMIM 136000).
One group described milia in association with multiple follicular hamartomas, vermiculate atrophoderma, hypotrichosis, and multiple basal cell carcinomas.

Milia have been reported with diseases including lichen planus, bullous pemphigoid, and contact dermatitis. They have also been associated with various medications including benoxaprofen, topical steroids, and nitrogen mustard in the treatment of mycosis fungoides. Milia can also occur after trauma, i.e., abrasions, burns, chemical peels, dermabrasion and excisional surgery.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Patients with various genodermatoses, blistering diseases, medication exposure, and trauma are at risk for developing milia

list.listitem: Milia are asymptomatic lesions. Typical lesions are shown in Images 1 and 2.
Usually, lesions are located on the eye, but occasionally they may be seen on the nose, areola, or genitalia.
Milia typically present as a firm, white, ≤3 mm keratin-filled cyst on the eyelids, cheeks, forehead, or genitalia.
In congenital milia, lesions tend to favor the nose, scalp, upper trunk, and upper extremities.
Epstein's pearls and Bohn's nodules are oral complements to milia of the skin.
Milia en plaque can present with erythematous plaques on the head and neck, classically in the preauricular area, studded with numerous milia.

Milia attributed to genodermatosis, underlying disease, medication, and trauma (secondary milia) appear clinically identical to benign primary milia. However, they are usually seen amongst a constitution of other findings.
Milia is a clinical diagnosis, hence diagnostic studies are generally not needed.
If diagnosis remains unclear, consider biopsy.
Perform a thorough history of lesion onset, duration, associated symptoms, underlying syndromes, diseases, medications, and trauma.
Diagnose lesion based on typical presentation.
If diagnosis is unclear, consider biopsy.
If removal is desired for cosmetic reasons, incision with a scalpel followed by expression of contents using a comedone extractor or curette may be performed. C
Post-extraction wound infection is rare but may be treated with topical mupirocin. B
Topical retinoids may be used in the treatment of multiple lesions.
Milia en plaque has been successfully treated with minocycline and oral retinoids.
Drug therapy is summarized in Table 1.
Milia are not injurious to one's health, and cosmesis remains the primary reason for treatment.

Incision of lesion with scalpel (#11 or #15 blade) or hypodermic needle (18-22 gauge) followed by evacuation of contents (with manual pressure, q-tips, curette, or a comedone extractor) is the treatment of choice, based on case reports and expert opinion.
Lesions have also been evacuated with the use of a paper clip and a hypodermic needle.
Fine needle electrodessication can be used successfully to treat milia and generally carries a very favorable cosmetic outcome.
Milia en plaque has been successfully treated with cryotherapy, electrodessication, dermabrasion, carbon dioxide laser, and erbium:YAG laser.
Extraction for a single lesion can be performed at the office visit or by patients themselves.
Topical retinoids, such as tretinoin 0.025%, adapalene 0.1%, or tazarotene 0.1% cream every night at bedtime for 1 to 2 months or until lesion resolves.
Advise patient to use gentle skin cleansers, emollients, and sunscreen daily while on long-term topical retinoid therapy, as xerosis/peeling and photosensitivity may occur.
Refer to dermatologist if the diagnosis is in doubt.
If milia is secondary to a genodermatosis or other disease, refer to the appropriate specialist.
To prevent infection, prep the area with 70% isopropyl alcohol prior to extraction.
Use a sterile scalpel or hypodermic needle for extraction.

Petrolatum or other healing ointment should be used to promote healing and minimize infection risk post-extraction. If infection does occur, mupirocin 2% ointment or cream should be applied TID for 10 days.
Congenital milia and oral inclusion cysts tend to resolve spontaneously within weeks to months. C
Benign primary milia in children and adults is usually more persistent that congenital milia. C
Secondary milia may persist indefinitely. C
